newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain urges calm in HK on China war anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Britain urges calm in HK on China war anniversary.

text.p: Britain called for calm in Hong Kong on Wednesday as anti-Japan protests whipped up by Tokyo's claim to disputed islands headed for a new high with rallies and candlelit vigils on a key war anniversary.
Senior Trade Commissioner Francis Cornish issued the plea as activists from the Chinese community marked the 65th anniversary of Japan's invasion of China with fresh protest actions against Tokyo.

September 18 is a painful date in the collective Chinese memory because the invasion of northeast China marked the start of a 14-year military carve-up by Japanese forces, accompanied by a string of war atrocities against Chinese civilians.
The memory is acute in Hong Kong, a British colony, because it was one of the territories occupied by Japan, from 1941 to 1945.

"...All of us understand that this is an issue that does arouse strong feelings," Cornish, formally Britain's Trade Commissioner, said. "These feelings should be expressed with restraint," he said in an interview on government radio.
"Things should not be allowed to get out of hand...nobody gains if this sort of thing starts to get out of control."

Anti-Japan protests have grown steadily over the past month, sparked by Japan's renewed claim to the East China Sea islands that China calls the Diaoyus and known in Japan as the Senkakus. Both countries claim the islands have been theirs for centuries.
On Wednesday a group of pro-democracy activists marched to China's mission in Hong Kong and successfully handed in a petition calling for firm action against Japan's claim.
A group of Hong Kong social workers marched to a Japanese school to demand that Japanese children be taught the truth about Japan's atrocities in World War Two.
They painted a picture of a crumpled Japanese military banner on the ground outside the school and urged pupils to resist a revival of Japanese militarism.

Another protest group marched into a Japanese department store in the prime shopping district of Causeway Bay shouting "don't buy Japanese goods". Management called in the police and evicted the protesters.

Passersby told reporters that they approved of the protests and the boycott call. Ships sounded their horns in Hong Kong harbour at noon as another mark of protest, and protest advertisements appeared in newspapers.
Hong Kong's biggest political party, the Democratic Party, and other groups planned to lead a rally and candlelit vigil in the evening to mark the invasion anniversary.
Protests in Hong Kong swelled last Sunday when more than 10,000 people gathered in the biggest action in a Chinese- populated territory so far during the campaign.
Smaller protests have taken place in Taiwan and Macau.
Hong Kong campaigners have gathered more than 760,000 signatures to protest against Japan's sovereignty claim. Japan's consulate has been flooded with petitions.
Hong Kong activists plan to sail to the islands next week to tear down a lighthouse erected by Japanese rightists.
The wave of patriotic nationalism has united usually opposing political forces, bridging the divide between pro-Beijing groups and anti-communist democrats.

"For the first time since the rift between them started, political activists in Hong Kong and the mainland government are united in a common cause and against a common adversary," one of China's Hong Kong advisers, Tsang Yok-sing, said.
Japan has claimed sovereign rights to the islands and has refused to acknowledge the dispute is open for discussion.
Tokyo's claim dates to 1895, when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories. China has also claimed sovereignty over the islands for centuries.
